developer_level: beginner-to-intermediate web developer with solid practical React/Next.js fundamentals and growing full-stack experience
moderate_knowledge: Next.js server-side and async data fetching
reusable button, badge and card components

coding_style.styling: Tailwind utility classes with DaisyUI where appropriate

preferred_patterns: Context with useState for appropriate shared state
TypeScript interfaces for props and data models
map, filter and some for straightforward collection logic
reusable components when UI is genuinely repeated
avoid_unnecessary_patterns: Redux or Zustand for simple shared state
TanStack Query or SWR for straightforward fetch requirements
repository, service or factory patterns for small applications without a real need
advanced TypeScript when simple interfaces are sufficient
new styling systems when Tailwind or DaisyUI already works
best-practice refactors that make familiar code harder to understand

new_concepts_policy.rule: Introduce new concepts when genuinely required by the project.
approach: Relate it to an existing familiar pattern when possible.
Do not hide substantial complexity behind abstractions.

agent_coding_rules: Match existing project patterns before introducing new ones.
Prefer the simplest solution that correctly solves the requirement.
Use React functional components and clear component boundaries.
Use useState for local state and Context with useState for appropriate shared state.
Prefer TypeScript interfaces for props, context and domain data.
Prefer direct fetch with async/await for ordinary API calls.
Use straightforward array methods for ordinary data transformations.
Prefer Tailwind and DaisyUI when already used by the project.
Keep abstractions proportional to project complexity.
Do not introduce libraries or architectural patterns without a concrete reason.
Do not assume missing dataset evidence means Fahim lacks that knowledge.
Do not assume advanced knowledge simply because a technology is being used.
Preserve established project style when modifying existing code.
When a new concept is genuinely necessary, explain it briefly.
Never make code unnecessarily clever when a straightforward implementation works.
Use advanced techniques when requirements genuinely require them, but explain why they are necessary.
